short_summary: The UK government has introduced a new code of practice for private car parks, offering drivers grace periods and clearer rules to prevent unfair fines.

sources.name: The Guardian
sources.title: Andy Burnham outlines new rules to outlaw ‘rip-off’ private parking fines

paragraphs: Motorists across England, Scotland, and Wales are set to receive new rights under an official code of practice designed to combat what authorities describe as exploitative parking charges. According to the prime minister, the regulations are part of a series of everyday fixes intended to ease the cost of living and ensure a fairer deal for consumers.

Under the proposed framework, drivers will be granted a guaranteed five-minute window to decide whether to park upon arrival. Furthermore, motorists will receive a 10-minute grace period to depart after their paid parking session concludes, protecting them from unexpected penalties before facing any fine.

The initiative comes in response to soaring numbers of tickets issued by private companies. Data from the RAC indicates that private firms distributed a record 16.9 million parking tickets during the 2025-26 period, representing a 17 percent increase in a single year. Complaints regarding the aggressive tactics and poor behavior of certain operators have persisted for years, with a previous attempt to implement a regulatory code in early 2022 collapsing following legal challenges from several parking firms that forced it to be withdrawn.

Despite the introduction of these measures, consumer organizations have expressed disappointment with certain aspects of the legislation. The consumer group Which? argued that the rules fall well short of what is necessary to help drivers fight back against parking cowboys effectively. Specifically, the government decided to maintain the existing maximum fine of £100 rather than halving it to £50, a reduction that consumer advocates and a previously withdrawn code had supported. Which? noted it was particularly concerning that the government had shied away from this £50 price cap.

Nevertheless, the new system introduces relief for specific types of errors. Fines will be dismissed entirely upon appeal when incurred through honest mistakes, including medical emergencies, vehicle breakdowns, broken ticket machines, or brief stops to check directions. For smaller slip-ups, such as entering an incorrect vehicle registration digit or forgetting to display a parking permit, the maximum appeal charge will be capped at £20. However, this appears to be a less generous system than under the original rules, which required the complete cancellation of a charge in all mitigating circumstances.

Additional concerns remain regarding independent appeals bodies and debt recovery fees. Which? pointed out that the government shied away from an independent appeals body capable of reining in the industry's worst practices. Furthermore, the consumer body highlighted that private parking debt recovery fees, which are regularly added without motorists' knowledge and push unfair charges even higher, were not immediately addressed. While these fees are currently capped at £70, the government has promised to consult on whether they should be cut or scrapped altogether as soon as possible next year. The new code is scheduled to be laid in parliament on Tuesday, though the exact date it will officially take effect remains to be determined, with ministers aiming to bring it into force as soon as possible.

facts.fact: A new private parking code of practice is due to be laid in parliament on Tuesday in the UK.
Drivers will receive a guaranteed five-minute grace period to decide whether to park and 10 minutes to leave after their session ends.
Private firms in the UK issued a record 16.9m parking tickets in 2025-26, according to the RAC.
The maximum parking charge will remain at £100, disappointing consumer groups like Which? that wanted a £50 cap.
Fines will be scrapped on appeal for honest mistakes such as medical emergencies, breakdowns, or broken ticket machines.
Smaller slip-ups like forgetting a permit or entering the wrong registration will face a maximum charge of £20 on appeal.
